section_summary: This section contains portions of the U.S. Embassy in Tokyo's comprehensive monthly report on political, diplomatic, and economic conditions in Japan for July 1941 (Report No. 1677), consisting of a duplicate copy fragment continuing from page 350 through page 370, followed by the complete formal Despatch No. 5812 dated August 25, 1941, from Ambassador Joseph C. Grew transmitting the full report and diplomatic communication schedules (pages 371–416). Major international developments covered include Japan's military occupation of southern French Indochina, the subsequent retaliatory freezing of Japanese assets by the United States, Great Britain, Canada, and the Netherlands East Indies, and representations concerning the bombing of Chungking and the endangering of the U.S.S. Tutuila. Domestically, the documents record the resignation of the Second Konoye Cabinet to drop Foreign Minister Yosuke Matsuoka, the formation of the Third Konoye Cabinet, large-scale army mobilization and deployments to Manchuria, stringent financial and trade regulations, and adverse agricultural conditions.

subfiles.about: Continuation of the Tokyo Embassy's monthly report on conditions in Japan during July 1941, covering international relations, cabinet reorganization, and economic developments.
subfiles.summary: This document contains pages 9 through 28 of Report No. 1677, continuing from the preceding section. It reviews Japan's relations with Great Britain, China, French Indochina, the Netherlands East Indies, the Soviet Union, and Mexico, highlighting the military entry into southern Indochina and subsequent Anglo-American and Dutch freezing of Japanese assets. It details the resignation of the Second Konoye Cabinet to remove Foreign Minister Yosuke Matsuoka, followed by the formation of the Third Konoye Cabinet with increased military representation. In addition, it discusses extensive military mobilization, the deployment of troops to Manchuria, comprehensive state financial and export licensing regulations, and poor agricultural harvests caused by unseasonable rains.
subfiles.title: Report of Conditions in Japan During the Month of July, 1941 (Report No. 1677, duplicate copy)

subfiles.about: Despatch No. 5812 transmitting Tokyo Embassy Report No. 1677 on conditions in Japan during July 1941, along with monthly schedules of telegrams and despatches.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Joseph C. Grew transmits to the Secretary of State the Tokyo Embassy's monthly report on political, economic, and international conditions in Japan for July 1941, accompanied by comprehensive indices of telegrams and despatches sent during that month. The report documents Japan's agreement with Vichy France for the joint defense and occupation of southern French Indochina, prompt asset-freezing countermeasures by the United States, Great Britain, Canada, and the Netherlands East Indies, and urgent diplomatic representations concerning the near-miss aerial bombing of the gunboat U.S.S. Tutuila at Chungking. It analyzes the fall of the Second Konoye Cabinet, the exclusion of Yosuke Matsuoka, the establishment of the Third Konoye Cabinet, and the strategic decisions reached at the Imperial Conference of July 2 regarding the German-Soviet conflict. Finally, it outlines massive nationwide troop mobilizations, reinforcements to Manchuria, stringent wartime economic and exchange controls, and agricultural difficulties resulting from severe spring and summer rains.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 5812: Report of Conditions in Japan During the Month of July, 1941
